query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is intended to retain the favorable mechanical performance of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi Cantor alloy while reducing cost and preserving a useful strength–ductility balance. Existing FeNiCrMn research has focused mainly on corrosion rather than dynamic loading. Molecular-dynamics studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys have examined temperature, strain rate, cracking, voids, and compositional variation, demonstrating condition-dependent mechanical responses, but they do not establish how to improve FeNiCrMn under dynamic loading. Given the constraints of remaining Co-free, controlling cost, and retaining balanced strength and ductility, what single intervention could improve the dynamic mechanical performance of FeNiCrMn over a defined range of temperatures and strain rates? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, the causal mechanism, a predicted outcome relative to unmodified FeNiCrMn, its boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of vanadium to the Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy will improve its dynamic mechanical performance over a defined range of temperatures and strain rates.
generation.conditions: Defined range of temperatures and strain rates
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a solid solution with vanadium
generation.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening and potential twinning-induced plasticity
generation.boundary: Temperature range: RT-1223 K, Strain rate range: 0.001-0.1 s−1
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of vanadium to be added and the resulting microstructure are uncertain

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of vanadium does not result in improved yield strength and ductility, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

The concept of multi-component high-entropy alloys (HEAs) has been presented in the beginning of this century. Most HEAs usually contain five elements with nearly equal atomic ratios []. HEAs have excellent mechanical properties, such as low strength and high plasticity [,,,,,,,,,,]. From recent literatures, the hardness of FeCoNiCrMn high-entropy alloy has even increased to 6700 MPa []. The Al0.6CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy also displayed the excellent strength–ductility combination for nanoscale deformation twins induced by dynamic loading and high-density dislocation substructure []. However, the NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy has still been regarded as a typical case for its single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) [] and relative promising mechanical properties. For example, its yield strength increases with the angle of rotation at high-pressure torsion (HPT) at room temperature at the cost of reduced ductility [] and can reach up to 350 MPa when reducing its grain size [,]. Understanding the mechanical properties of the Cantor alloy has been the subject of active research efforts. Its elastic constants, determined using experimental, and computational techniques, have been found to exhibit similar elastic anisotropy as Fe. Further, the Cantor alloy was found to exhibit simultaneous mechanical strength and ductility,,, with yield strength values that are comparable to Ni-based superalloys and steels, but lower than aluminum-containing and refractory metal-based HEAs,. Gali and George have shown that the yield and ultimate strengths and ductility all increase simultaneously with decreasing temperature down to 77 K. The lack of tradeoff between strength and ductility and the exceptional fracture-toughness of the Cantor alloy at low temperatures have been attributed to deformation induced nanotwinning as an additional mode of plastic deformation,,,.
